name: Ditransitive VP (Double-object Construction)

dimensions.form: VP headed by a verb with two internal core complements: indirect object followed by direct object
dimensions.meaning: Role alignment is centred on recipient and theme, but extends to goods-beneficiary, prevention, source, loss, and other affected-participant interpretations
dimensions.function: Packages two participants as indirect and direct object
dimensions.distribution: Licensed by particular verb senses; many, but not all, have a related monotransitive VP with a to- or for-PP

1.definition: The indirect object denotes a recipient of the entity, information, or experience denoted by the direct object
1.details: CGEL defines ditransitive complementation syntactically for clauses and verb uses by Oi + Od; both objects are internal to the VP and licensed by its head verb. This entry records that complementation pattern at VP level, not a necessary caused-possession meaning. Goldberg instead organizes the double-object pattern around a caused-receipt or giving prototype with related extensions (CGEL Ch. 4 §§1–1.1, 4.3, 8.2, pp. 215–17, 248–51, 308–13; Goldberg 2006: 20–28).

2.definition: The indirect object denotes the intended beneficiary or recipient of goods created or obtained
2.details: CGEL restricts the central beneficiary alternation mainly to beneficiaries of goods rather than services; the interpretation normally includes intended transfer of the direct-object referent (CGEL pp. 310–11).

examples.note: Goods-beneficiary use; contrast service-beneficiary *I'll do you the washing-up

3.definition: The indirect object denotes a prevented recipient, source, loser, or other affected participant rather than an actual recipient
3.details: These participants are still indirect objects on syntactic evidence. CGEL includes Oi-only permission and refusal verbs and source-role uses of charge, cost, and fine (pp. 309, 311–13); Goldberg analyzes prevented receipt and loss as extensions of the giving prototype.

examples.note: Ed is source rather than recipient

constraints.description: Licensing is lexeme- and sense-specific: give allows Oi or to, explain is to-only, buy allows Oi or for, borrow is for-only, and spare has Oi-only senses.
In the canonical VP, Oi precedes Od. Some chiefly BrE varieties allow Od–Oi when both are personal pronouns, as in He gave it her.
A to- or for-PP is not an indirect object. In sent a copy to Sue, the VP is monotransitive: a copy is Od, the to-PP is a complement, and Sue is oblique within that PP.
With only one object in a canonical active VP, that object is Od even when its semantic role corresponds to the Oi of a ditransitive alternant.
Recipient, animacy, and caused receipt are central tendencies, not necessary conditions for membership in the CGEL syntactic class.

projection.target: A verb sense attested in the canonical Head–NP–NP frame predicts reduced frontability and postposability of the first NP relative to the second, preference for first-object passivization, and an animate, given, and topical bias in the first-object slot
projection.evidence: CGEL documents fixed order and extraction asymmetries on pp. 248–50, passive asymmetries on pp. 249–50, information-packaging preferences on pp. 309–10, and role and alternant classes on pp. 308–13

grounds.note: Order, extraction, passive, information-packaging, and alternant diagnostics
The Oi/Od asymmetries recur across independently defined verb-sense classes

core.property: Two internal core-complement objects, Oi and Od
diagnostics: contrast with Od plus PP and Od plus predicative complement
Oi-or-to, to-only, Oi-or-for, for-only, and Oi-only lexical classes

peripheral.property: Recipient or goods-beneficiary bias for Oi

diagnostics: Od plus to-PP or for-PP for many, but not all, verb senses
Oi-corresponding passive subject generally preferred over Od-corresponding passive subject

activation_states.context: Both objects are personal pronouns in some BrE varieties

activation_states.effect: Passive acceptability is generally lower and more speaker-variable

variation.speaker_variation: Judgements vary for second passives, for-beneficiary passives, and some service-beneficiary double-object VPs.

known_boundary_items: sent a copy to Sue: Od plus PP, hence monotransitive, not ditransitive
considered Ed a fool: Od plus NP predicative complement, not two objects
sent Kim to the back: Od plus locative-goal PP, hence monotransitive and not ditransitive
teaches the students: its sole object is Od despite matching the semantic role of a ditransitive Oi

relatedConstructions.notes: Ditransitive complementation is a specialization of VP structure
The two object slots are normally realized by NPs
Caused motion has one Od plus a locative PP complement and is therefore monotransitive, not ditransitive

grounds.note: Ditransitive complementation is the syntactic Head-Oi-Od pattern, not a semantic transfer class
Caused-receipt prototype and extensions in the double-object semantic network

curious.title: Verbs that take two objects
curious.summary: Some verbs can be followed by two noun phrases in a row, such as someone who receives and the thing received.
curious.body:
In I sent Sue a copy, the verb sent is followed by two things: Sue, who gets the copy, and a copy, what is sent. The first is called the indirect object and the second the direct object. Each is a full noun phrase, and the verb allows both.

The pattern isn't only about handing things over. It also fits She baked Kim a cake, where the cake is meant for Kim, and It cost Mel his job, where Mel loses something. Which verbs allow it depends on the verb: some also allow a version with to or for, as in I sent a copy to Sue, and some don't.
curious.try: Say I sent Sue a copy, then say I sent a copy to Sue. Does the meaning change? Now try the same with other verbs, such as baked or told.

teacher.summary: Helps explain double-object verbs, what counts as an indirect object, and how they differ from verbs with a to- or for-phrase.
teacher.explain: A ditransitive VP has a verb followed by two internal objects, the indirect object (Oi) and then the direct object (Od), as in sent Sue a copy. This dictionary treats this as a syntactic pattern, not a meaning class: the Oi tends to be a recipient or beneficiary of goods, but can also be a prevented recipient, a source or a loser (refused Kim permission, charged Ed ten dollars, cost Mel his job). Which verb senses allow it is lexically specific: give allows Oi or a to-phrase, explain takes only to, buy allows Oi or for, and borrow takes only for. A to- or for-phrase is not an indirect object: in sent a copy to Sue, a copy is the direct object and the verb is monotransitive.
teacher.terms: Indirect object and direct object are the usual terms. Double-object construction is another name for the same pattern.

contrasts.text: I sent a copy to Sue.
contrasts.note: One object plus a to-phrase; monotransitive.
One object plus a predicative NP, not two objects.

watch_for: A learner might treat the to-phrase in sent a copy to Sue as an indirect object.
A learner might assume any verb that can take a to-phrase can also take two objects, though licensing depends on the verb sense.
A learner might read the two NPs in considered Ed a fool as two objects, when a fool describes Ed.
teacher.activity: Give students verb cards (give, send, bake, explain, buy). They try each in a double-object sentence and in a to- or for-phrase sentence, sort the results, and compare with a dictionary or the teacher.

child.hook: Can you give a friend a pencil without saying "to"?
child.explain: Some verbs can be followed by who something is for and then the thing itself. Dad baked Kim a cake. The cake is meant for Kim. The words come in that order.
child.play: Make up sentences with who gets something, then what they get. Try sent, told and baked. Then say each one again with to or for and a name at the end.
